chapters.name: Chapter 1: Using AI tools for teacher tasks

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The kinds of AI tools in schools
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort AI tools into general assistants, education platforms and built-in features.
This lesson builds toward: Given the AI tools your staff use, you will sort each tool into general assistant, education platform or built-in feature, marking whether the district has an agreement for it.
General AI assistants, such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and Claude, can do almost any writing or thinking task. They are flexible, but they know nothing about your curriculum unless you tell them, and their data terms depend on which plan you use.
Education AI platforms are built for teachers or students: lesson and quiz generators, tutoring tools, feedback tools. They may fit school tasks better and some offer district agreements, but each must be vetted for privacy and quality.
Built-in AI features live inside tools you already use: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Canva, your learning management system. They are convenient, but they may be switched on without anyone deciding to, so check with your technology team which are on and under what agreement.
Words to know:
- General assistant: an AI chat tool that can help with almost any task.
- Education platform: an AI tool made for teaching or learning tasks.
- Built-in feature: an AI function inside software you already use.
Try it now: List the AI tools you or your staff use now. Put each in one of the three kinds, and mark whether your district has an agreement for it (yes, no, don't know).
You can now sort AI tools into three kinds and know what to check for each.

check.q: What is a built-in AI feature?
options: An AI tool you must buy separately
An AI feature inside software you already use
A chatbot made by a student
A paper worksheet
check.why: Built-in features appear inside tools you already own, sometimes switched on by default.

check.q: A teacher uses a new education AI platform you have not heard of. What would you do first?
options: Approve it, since it is made for schools
Ban all AI platforms
List it and check whether the district has an agreement for it
Ask students if they like it
check.why: Education platforms still need to be vetted for privacy and quality.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A prompt pattern that works for teachers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write teacher prompts with role, learners, goal, constraints and format.
This lesson builds toward: For a lesson you teach or support, you will write a teacher prompt with role, learners, goal, constraints and format, with all five parts and saved on a shared prompt card.
Teachers get better results with a five-part prompt. Role: "You are an experienced 7th-grade science teacher." Learners: grade, reading level, needs in general terms (no names). Goal: the learning objective or standard. Constraints: time, materials, length, what to avoid. Format: a table, numbered steps, a handout.
Example: "You are an experienced 4th-grade teacher. My class reads at a range of levels. Write a 300-word passage about the water cycle at three reading levels with the same key facts, then five comprehension questions for each. Use a table."
Then improve it with follow-ups: "make level 1 simpler", "add a vocabulary list", "align questions to the main idea". Save prompts that work on a shared prompt card so colleagues can reuse them.
Step by step:
- Role: who should the AI act as?
- Learners: grade, level, needs in general terms.
- Goal: objective or standard.
- Constraints: time, length, materials.
- Format: table, steps, handout.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type to an AI tool to ask for something.
- Prompt card: a shared list of tested prompts staff can reuse.
Try it now: Write a five-part prompt for a lesson you will teach (or support) soon. Run it, ask one follow-up, and save the final prompt.
You can now write teacher prompts that get usable results the first time.

check.q: What goes in the "constraints" part of a teacher prompt?
options: Limits such as length, reading level or what to avoid
The student's full name
The teacher's password
The name of the AI tool
check.why: Constraints set limits so the answer fits your class.

check.q: AI gives a passage that is too hard for your students. What would you send?
options: Start over in a new tool
Accept it and explain the hard words in class
Paste a student's reading scores
A follow-up such as "Make it simpler, with shorter sentences"
check.why: A clear follow-up adjusts the answer without sharing student data.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Three everyday tasks, done well
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI for a parent email, a leveled passage and practice questions, and check each.
This lesson builds toward: Using made-up details, you will use AI for a parent email, a leveled passage and practice questions with an answer key, and check each, fixing every error before use and working every answer yourself.
Parent email: give the purpose, the key facts (event, date, what families need to do) and the tone. Ask for a short, warm version in plain English. If it must go out in other languages, an AI translation is a draft; have a qualified speaker check it before it reaches families.
Leveled passage: ask for the same content at three reading levels with the same key facts. Check the facts yourself; AI can introduce errors when it simplifies.
Practice questions: ask for ten questions with an answer key and a short explanation for each answer. Work the answers yourself; AI answer keys are wrong more often than people expect, especially in math and science. In all three, you are the editor and the final check.
Step by step:
- Parent email: purpose, facts, tone; translation checked by a qualified person.
- Leveled passage: same facts at three levels; check the facts.
- Practice questions: answer key with explanations; work every answer yourself.
- Edit everything before it is used.
Words to know:
- Leveled text: the same content written at different reading levels.
- Answer key: the list of correct answers for questions.
Try it now: Do all three tasks with made-up details: a parent email about a field trip, a passage at three levels, and ten questions with an answer key. Count the errors you had to fix.
You can now use AI for three everyday teacher tasks and check the results like an editor.

options: Text printed in large letters
The same content written at different reading levels
A text with no pictures
A test with three sections
check.why: Leveled text lets students at different reading levels learn the same content.

check.q: AI writes ten practice questions with an answer key. What do you do before using them?
options: Work every answer yourself and fix errors
Use them as they are
Check only the first question
Ask the AI if its answers are right
check.why: AI answer keys are wrong more often than people expect, so the teacher checks every one.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Choosing tools that are safe for students

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading a tool's privacy terms with a checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check an AI tool's privacy policy and terms against a short checklist.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI tool staff want, you will check its privacy policy and terms against a privacy checklist, marking each item clear, unclear or a problem for the plan you would use.
The US Department of Education's Student Privacy Policy Office publishes a Model Terms of Service checklist to help schools review an online tool's privacy policy and terms before signing up. Use it, or a checklist your district already has.
Key questions: What student data does it collect? Who owns the data? Does the company use student data for advertising or to train its AI models? Can the school get data deleted, and when? Who else gets the data? How is it protected, and what happens if there is a breach? Can the company change the terms without telling you?
Read the policy for the plan you would actually use; free consumer plans and education plans often have different terms. If the answers are unclear, the answer is "not yet". FERPA and COPPA set the floor, and your state may have stricter student-privacy laws; your district's privacy officer can tell you which apply.
Step by step:
- Open the tool's privacy policy and terms for the plan you would use.
- Go through the checklist: data collected, ownership, ads and training, deletion, sharing, security, changes.
- Mark each item clear, unclear or a problem.
- Ask the vendor about unclear items in writing.
- Send the result to your district privacy officer.
Words to know:
- Privacy policy: a company's statement of what data it collects and how it uses it.
- Terms of service: the rules and agreement for using a product.
- Data breach: when data is accessed or released without permission.
Official sources:
- Privacy and Education Technology: Model Terms of Service checklist
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
Try it now: Pick one AI tool your staff want. Read its privacy policy for the plan you would use and mark each checklist item clear, unclear or a problem.
You can now vet an AI tool's privacy terms with a checklist before it is used with students.

check.q: Which is a privacy checklist question?
options: Is the tool's logo friendly?
How many people use it?
Does the company use student data to train its AI?
Does it work on tablets?
check.why: Whether student data trains the AI is a key privacy question.

check.q: The free plan's privacy terms differ from the education plan's. Which do you check?
options: Whichever is shorter
The free plan, since it is cheaper
Neither; terms are all the same
The terms for the plan your school would actually use
check.why: Free consumer and education plans often have different terms.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Age rules and student accounts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a tool's age rules and how COPPA applies before students sign in.
This lesson builds toward: Before students sign in to a tool, you will check the tool's current minimum age and parental-permission rules and how COPPA applies, using the tool's own current terms.
Many AI tools set minimum ages and parental-permission rules in their terms, and these change. Check each tool's current terms; do not rely on what a colleague remembers. A tool that is fine for teachers may not be allowed for students at all.
For children under 13, COPPA applies to the online service. The FTC says a school may consent in place of parents only when the service collects student information for the use and benefit of the school and for no other commercial purpose. The FTC also suggests, as good practice, that schools tell parents which online services they have approved.
Prefer school-managed student accounts under a district agreement over students signing up on their own with personal emails. Decide in advance what students may use AI for, and tell families.
Step by step:
- Read the tool's current age and permission rules.
- If students are under 13, check how COPPA consent would work.
- Prefer school-managed accounts under an agreement.
- Tell families which services are approved.
- Decide what students may use it for.
Words to know:
- Minimum age: the youngest age a tool's terms allow to use it.
- School-managed account: a student account created and controlled by the school.
Official sources:
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: For the tool from Lesson 4, find its current minimum age and parental-permission rule in its terms. Write whether students in your school could use it, and how.
You can now check a tool's age rules and COPPA consent before any student signs in.

check.q: How should student accounts on an AI tool preferably be set up?
options: Students sign up with personal email
Teachers share one login with the class
School-managed accounts under an agreement
No accounts; students use a parent's account
check.why: School-managed accounts under an agreement keep student data under the school's control.

check.q: A colleague says a tool is fine for 10-year-olds. What do you check?
options: The tool's current terms for its minimum age and parental-permission rule
A review on social media
Whether other schools use it
Nothing; trust the colleague
check.why: Age rules change, so check the tool's current terms yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Publishing a green-yellow-red tools list
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Publish a simple list that tells staff which AI tools are approved and for what.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least three vetted tools, you will publish a green-yellow-red tools list for staff, showing each tool's color, reason, allowed uses and date checked.
Staff need a simple answer to "can I use this?". A green-yellow-red list gives it. Green: approved under a district agreement, may be used with student information as the agreement allows. Yellow: allowed for teacher tasks with no student information (lesson ideas, generic materials). Red: not allowed, because of privacy, age or quality problems.
For each tool, record the color, the reason, the allowed uses, whether students may use it, and the date you checked. Your district's privacy officer or technology team should agree with the green list.
Pair the list with your prompt card so staff know both what to use and how to use it well. Review both each term, because tools and terms change.
Step by step:
- List the tools you checked.
- Give each a color: green, yellow or red.
- Write the reason, allowed uses, student use and date checked.
- Get the privacy officer or technology team to confirm.
- Share it with the prompt card; review each term.
Words to know:
- Approved list: a published list of tools staff may use and how.
- Agreement: a signed contract or data-privacy agreement between the district and a company.
Try it now: Final task: build your starter toolkit, a prompt card with your three tested prompts (parent email, leveled passage, practice questions) and a green-yellow-red list of at least three tools checked with the privacy checklist, each with a one-line reason.
You can now give staff a trusted, simple guide to which AI tools to use and how to use them.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Prompt card Fewer than three prompts, or prompts are missing parts. Three tested prompts (parent email, leveled passage, practice questions) with role, learners, goal, constraints and format. Each prompt includes a useful follow-up that staff can reuse. Outputs checked Outputs were used without checking, or the answer key was not worked. Each output was checked and errors fixed; every answer in the key was worked. Notes how many errors were found and what kind. Privacy checklist Tools were not checked, or the checklist is not based on the Model Terms of Service resource. Each tool was checked with a privacy checklist built from the Model Terms of Service resource on studentprivacy.ed.gov. Unclear items were sent to the vendor as written questions. Age rules Student use is allowed without checking age rules. Notes each tool's current minimum age and parental-permission rule from its terms. Explains how students could use it, such as school-managed accounts. Green-yellow-red list Fewer than three tools, or colors without reasons. At least three tools, each with a color and a one-line reason. Also shows allowed uses and date checked, and was sent to the privacy officer or technology team to confirm. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a GREEN tool mean on the list?
options: It is free
It may be used, including with student information as the district agreement allows
It is banned
Only students may use it
check.why: Green tools are approved, and student information is allowed only as the agreement allows.

check.q: A tool's terms changed since your list was made. What would you do?
options: Leave the list as it is until next year
Delete the whole list
Recheck the tool, update its color and the date checked
Tell staff to decide for themselves
check.why: The list shows a date checked so it stays current as terms change.
